gloss: A blockage that stops things from moving forward, originally a mass of floating logs stuck in a river.
examples: The bill is stuck in a *logjam* in the Senate.
Crews worked all morning to break up the *logjam* on the river.
A few small concessions finally cleared the *logjam*.

gloss: A person who prefers to be alone rather than with other people.
examples: He was always a *loner* in high school.
Most *loners* aren't unhappy — they just like their own company.
Neighbors described the suspect as a quiet *loner*.

gloss: A very tall bow drawn by hand, used in medieval warfare and still used in archery.
examples: English archers won the battle with the *longbow*.
He shoots a wooden *longbow* rather than a modern compound bow.
The museum displays several *longbows* from the fifteenth century.

gloss: Long life, or the length of time that someone or something lasts.
examples: Diet and exercise both affect *longevity*.
The band is known for its *longevity* — forty years on the road.
Researchers study *longevity* in small island populations.

gloss: Ordinary handwriting, as opposed to shorthand or typing.
examples: She wrote the whole draft in *longhand* before typing it.
His notes were in *longhand* and hard to read.
The essay portion has to be answered in *longhand*.

gloss: A breed of cattle with very long horns, raised especially in Texas.
examples: A herd of *longhorns* grazed along the highway.
The ranch still raises Texas *longhorns*.
A *longhorn* skull hung above the fireplace.

gloss: Money and goods taken by force or theft.
examples: The thieves hid the *loot* in a storage unit.
Soldiers carried off the *loot* from the palace.
He spent an hour sorting through the *loot* he'd picked up in the game.
contrast: Sounds exactly like lute. Loot is stolen goods; a lute is a musical instrument.

gloss: A man of high rank in Britain, or a ruler with power over land and people.
examples: The castle belonged to a powerful *lord*.
Several *lords* voted against the measure.
He acts like the *lord* of the manor.

gloss: Traditional knowledge and stories about a subject, passed down over time.
examples: Local *lore* says the lake has no bottom.
The game has a deep *lore* that fans argue about online.
She grew up on family *lore* about the old country.

gloss: A large vehicle for carrying goods by road — the British word for a truck.
examples: A *lorry* blocked the narrow street in the village.
The report said two *lorries* had overturned on the motorway.
In America you'd call that *lorry* a truck.
contrast: British only. Americans say truck, and a British lorry driver is an American truck driver.

gloss: Someone who does not win, or an unsuccessful and unpopular person.
examples: The *loser* of the match still made the finals.
Don't be a sore *loser*.
He dismissed his critics as a bunch of *losers*.
contrast: One o: loser /ˈluːzər/, with a z sound. Two o's makes looser /ˈluːsər/, 'less tight', with an s sound.

gloss: A game in which numbered tickets are sold and prizes go to the numbers drawn at random.
examples: She won the state *lottery* twice.
Getting a good teacher can feel like a *lottery*.
Most states run their own *lotteries*.

gloss: A lottery game in which players pick a set of numbers and hope they match the ones drawn.
examples: He plays *lotto* every Friday.
The *lotto* jackpot rolled over to ninety million dollars.
My grandmother buys *lotto* tickets at the corner store.

gloss: A water plant with large flat leaves and big pink or white flowers, important in Asian art and religion.
examples: Pink *lotuses* covered the surface of the pond.
She sat cross-legged in the *lotus* position.
A carved *lotus* decorated the temple wall.

gloss: Someone who talks too much and too loudly, often saying things better left unsaid.
examples: The guy at the next table was a real *loudmouth*.
A couple of *loudmouths* ruined the meeting.
Don't tell him anything — he's a *loudmouth*.

gloss: A device that turns an electrical signal into sound loud enough for a crowd to hear.
examples: An announcement came over the *loudspeaker*.
The *loudspeakers* at the stadium were deafening.
He wired a pair of *loudspeakers* to the amplifier.

gloss: Comfortable, casual clothing meant for relaxing at home.
examples: She lives in *loungewear* on the weekends.
The *loungewear* section is right next to the pajamas.
Sales of *loungewear* jumped when everyone started working from home.

gloss: A small parrot that stays close to its mate, and informally one of a pair of people obviously in love.
examples: The two *lovebirds* held hands the whole flight.
She keeps a pair of *lovebirds* in a cage by the window.
Look at those *lovebirds* in the back booth.

gloss: Someone you are in a romantic or sexual relationship with, or a person who is very fond of something.
examples: She took a *lover* while her husband was overseas.
He's a great *lover* of jazz.
The park is full of dog *lovers* on Saturday mornings.

gloss: An area of land that is lower and flatter than the country around it.
examples: The river floods the *lowlands* every spring.
Rice grows well in the coastal *lowland*.
Fog settles in the *lowlands* overnight.

gloss: Someone who stays loyal to a government, ruler, or leader, especially when others turn against it.
examples: The town was full of *loyalists* during the revolution.
A handful of *loyalists* stayed with the senator after the scandal.
*Loyalist* troops held the capital for a week.

gloss: A small medicated tablet that dissolves slowly in the mouth to soothe a sore throat.
examples: Take a *lozenge* if your throat hurts.
She keeps cough *lozenges* in her purse.
The *lozenge* tasted like honey and lemon.

gloss: The use of oil or grease to make moving parts slide smoothly against each other.
examples: The engine seized from a lack of *lubrication*.
Proper *lubrication* keeps the chain from rusting.
The manual explains the *lubrication* schedule.

gloss: A winter sport in which racers slide down an icy track lying face up on a small sled.
examples: She won a bronze medal in the *luge*.
*Luge* is one of the fastest sports at the Winter Olympics.
He crashed on his second *luge* run.

gloss: A person whose job is cutting down trees for timber.
examples: His grandfather worked as a *lumberjack* in Maine.
The *lumberjacks* felled the tree in under a minute.
He showed up in a plaid *lumberjack* shirt.

gloss: A business that stores and sells cut wood and building materials.
examples: We picked up the plywood at the *lumberyard*.
There's a *lumberyard* out on Route 9.
Both *lumberyards* in town closed last year.

gloss: A person who is famous and widely respected in a particular field.
examples: The conference drew *luminaries* from across the industry.
She's a *luminary* in cancer research.
A few literary *luminaries* sat in the front row.

gloss: Extremely foolish or reckless behavior.
examples: Driving through that storm was sheer *lunacy*.
He called the plan economic *lunacy*.
It would be *lunacy* to quit now.

gloss: Someone who behaves in a wild, dangerous, or completely unreasonable way.
examples: Some *lunatic* passed us on the shoulder.
He drove like a *lunatic* the whole way home.
The *lunatics* are running the asylum.

gloss: A room in a school or workplace where people eat their midday meal.
examples: The kids eat in the school *lunchroom*.
She microwaved her soup in the office *lunchroom*.
Both *lunchrooms* were packed at noon.

gloss: A sudden forward movement of the body, or an exercise in which you step forward and bend the front knee.
examples: He made a *lunge* for the ball and missed.
Do three sets of *lunges* on each leg.
The dog's *lunge* pulled the leash right out of her hand.

gloss: A long-term autoimmune disease in which the body attacks its own tissues, often causing a rash and joint pain.
examples: She was diagnosed with *lupus* at twenty-six.
*Lupus* can be very hard to diagnose.
He takes medication to keep the *lupus* under control.

gloss: A sudden, uncontrolled tilt or jerking movement to one side.
examples: The bus started with a *lurch*.
A *lurch* of the boat sent the coffee across the table.
He quit without notice and left us in the *lurch*.

ru: пассивный участник форума, читатель без комментариев
gloss: Someone who reads an online forum or chat regularly without ever posting anything.
examples: Most of the group are *lurkers* who never comment.
I was a *lurker* on that message board for years.
Long-time *lurker*, first-time poster.

gloss: An old stringed instrument with a rounded back and a bent-back neck, played by plucking.
examples: He played a Renaissance dance on the *lute*.
The museum has three sixteenth-century *lutes*.
A *lute* sounds softer and rounder than a guitar.
contrast: Sounds exactly like loot. A lute is an instrument; loot is stolen goods.

gloss: The clear fluid that carries white blood cells through its own network of vessels in the body.
examples: *Lymph* drains through the nodes in your neck.
Swelling happens when *lymph* can't flow freely.
The doctor checked the *lymph* nodes under his arm.

gloss: A cancer that begins in the cells of the lymphatic system.
examples: He was treated for *lymphoma* in his twenties.
The scan showed *lymphoma* in two lymph nodes.
*Lymphoma* responds well to chemotherapy in many cases.

gloss: The killing of someone by a mob without a trial, especially by hanging.
examples: The museum documents thousands of *lynchings* in the South.
A historical marker names the victims of the 1919 *lynching*.
The *lynching* went unpunished for a century.

gloss: An ancient Greek stringed instrument shaped like a small U-shaped harp.
examples: The poet is shown holding a *lyre*.
Two bronze *lyres* sat in the museum case.
He plucked a few notes on the *lyre*.
contrast: Sounds exactly like liar. Different spelling, different meaning.

gloss: A person who writes the words for songs.
examples: He's the band's guitarist and *lyricist*.
The show's composer and *lyricist* both won awards.
Great *lyricists* make ordinary words sound new.

gloss: A round, rich, buttery nut from an Australian tree, or the tree itself.
examples: She baked white chocolate and *macadamia* cookies.
A handful of *macadamias* costs more than a whole bag of peanuts.
*Macadamias* are grown commercially in Hawaii.

gloss: A short-tailed monkey found across Asia and North Africa, common in zoos and in research.
examples: A troop of *macaques* raided the picnic tables.
The *macaque* stared right into the camera.
Japanese *macaques* bathe in hot springs in winter.

gloss: Short curved tubes of pasta, often baked with cheese.
examples: The kids want *macaroni* and cheese again.
Boil the *macaroni* for about eight minutes.
She brought a big bowl of *macaroni* salad.
contrast: Uncountable in English and it names one specific shape — unlike Russian макароны, which is plural and covers pasta in general.

gloss: A small chewy cookie made from egg whites with shredded coconut or ground almonds.
examples: She baked coconut *macaroons* for the holiday.
Each *macaroon* was dipped in dark chocolate.
The *macaroons* went fast at the bake sale.
contrast: Not a macaron (mak-uh-RAHN), the smooth French sandwich cookie made with almond flour. Two cookies, two spellings.

gloss: A heavy club with a spiked or knobbed metal head, used as a medieval weapon and now carried as a ceremonial staff.
examples: The knight swung a *mace* instead of a sword.
Two ceremonial *maces* stood beside the speaker's chair.
A *mace* could crush armor that a blade couldn't cut.

gloss: An exaggerated show of masculine pride and toughness.
examples: The locker room reeked of *machismo*.
His *machismo* kept him from asking for help.
The film is a study in small-town *machismo*.

gloss: The craft of knotting cord into decorative patterns such as plant hangers and wall pieces.
examples: She hung a *macrame* plant holder in the window.
He's taking a *macrame* class at the community center.
The walls were covered in seventies *macrame*.

gloss: A single command or key combination that runs a saved sequence of steps in a program.
examples: I wrote a *macro* to format the report automatically.
Word won't run *macros* from files it doesn't trust.
Record a *macro* instead of doing it by hand every week.

gloss: A formal, polite way to address a woman whose name you do not know.
examples: Can I help you, *madam*?
The letter began, "Dear Sir or *Madam*."
"Right away, *madam*," the waiter said.
contrast: In everyday American speech the form is ma'am; madam is reserved for formal writing and titles like Madam Chair.

gloss: Wildly foolish behavior, or a state of severe mental illness.
examples: Driving through that traffic was pure *madness*.
It would be *madness* to put everything into one stock.
There's a method to his *madness*.

gloss: A secret criminal organization that runs extortion, smuggling, and other rackets.
examples: The *mafia* controlled the docks for decades.
Local *mafias* fought over the construction contracts.
He testified against the *mafia* and entered witness protection.

gloss: A member of the Mafia.
examples: He plays an aging *mafioso* in the new film.
Three *mafiosi* were arrested in the raid.
The witness described the *mafioso* who ran the neighborhood.
contrast: Irregular Italian plural: one mafioso, several mafiosi — not "mafiosos".

gloss: A judge who handles minor cases and preliminary hearings in a lower court.
examples: A federal *magistrate* set bail at fifty thousand dollars.
The case went before a *magistrate* on Monday.
Two *magistrates* signed the search warrant.

gloss: Hot molten rock beneath the earth's surface.
examples: *Magma* rose into the chamber under the volcano.
The island was built up by cooling *magma*.
Seismographs track the movement of *magma*.
contrast: Underground it is magma; once it reaches the surface the same rock is called lava.

gloss: Impressive beauty, scale, or splendor.
examples: Nothing prepares you for the *magnificence* of the canyon.
The cathedral's *magnificence* took her breath away.
He wrote a whole chapter on the *magnificence* of the old court.

gloss: A lens or device that makes things look bigger.
examples: She reads the fine print with a *magnifier*.
The phone has a built-in screen *magnifier*.
Jewelers use small handheld *magnifiers*.

gloss: A hard reddish-brown tropical wood used for fine furniture.
examples: The desk is solid *mahogany*.
She stained the pine to look like *mahogany*.
*Mahogany* darkens as it ages.

gloss: A man whose job is delivering mail to homes and businesses.
examples: The *mailman* comes around two o'clock.
Our *mailman* knows every dog on the route.
Two *mailmen* split the neighborhood.
contrast: Irregular plural: mailmen. The neutral American term is mail carrier; the British word is postman.

gloss: A large, powerful computer used by big organizations to process huge amounts of data.
examples: The bank still runs payroll on a *mainframe*.
Old *mainframes* filled entire rooms.
He writes COBOL for a *mainframe*.

gloss: The main landmass of a country or continent, as opposed to its islands.
examples: A ferry runs to the *mainland* twice a day.
She moved from the island to the *mainland* for work.
Groceries are cheaper on the *mainland*.

gloss: The person or thing that something depends on most.
examples: Tourism is the *mainstay* of the local economy.
He was a *mainstay* of the defense for ten years.
Rice and beans are the *mainstays* of the diet here.

gloss: A person or company that makes something.
examples: The car *maker* recalled thirty thousand vehicles.
She's a furniture *maker* in Vermont.
Several drug *makers* cut their prices this year.

gloss: An illness, or a serious problem in a society or system.
examples: He suffered from a mysterious *malady* for years.
Corruption is the country's oldest *malady*.
The report lists the *maladies* of the health system.

gloss: A vague feeling of illness or unease, or a period of low spirits and weak activity.
examples: A general *malaise* settled over the office.
The first symptoms are fatigue and *malaise*.
Economists blamed the *malaise* on falling wages.

gloss: A serious disease spread by mosquito bites, causing recurring fever and chills.
examples: He caught *malaria* while working in the tropics.
Bed nets cut *malaria* deaths sharply.
She takes pills to prevent *malaria*.

gloss: A person or animal of the sex that fathers young.
examples: The clinic treats both *males* and females.
The *male* builds the nest and the female lines it.
Adult *males* are about twice the size of the females.
contrast: Sounds exactly like mail (letters and packages).

gloss: A failure of a machine or system to work the way it should.
examples: A software *malfunction* grounded the flights.
The recall covers a brake *malfunction*.
Two *malfunctions* in one week is too many.

gloss: The wish to harm someone, or the deliberate intent behind a hurtful act.
examples: She said it without any *malice*.
The jury found *malice* in the defendant's actions.
There isn't an ounce of *malice* in him.

gloss: A common wild duck; the male has a glossy green head and a white ring around its neck.
examples: A pair of *mallards* landed on the pond.
The *mallard* dabbled at the edge of the reeds.
*Mallards* winter on the lake by the thousands.

gloss: A hammer with a large head of wood, rubber, or plastic, used where a metal hammer would damage the surface.
examples: Tap the joint together with a rubber *mallet*.
He carved the bowl with a chisel and a wooden *mallet*.
The croquet set came with six *mallets*.

gloss: Poor health caused by not eating enough food or not eating the right kinds of food.
examples: The children showed clear signs of *malnutrition*.
Aid groups are fighting *malnutrition* across the region.
*Malnutrition* can happen even where food is plentiful.

gloss: Careless or illegal conduct by a professional, especially a doctor or lawyer, that harms a patient or client.
examples: The family sued the hospital for *malpractice*.
Every surgeon carries *malpractice* insurance.
The board found no evidence of *malpractice*.

gloss: An informal or childlike word for mother.
examples: The baby cried for her *mama*.
Tell your *mama* I said hello.
The *mamas* in the neighborhood organized the whole thing.

gloss: A long, fast, highly venomous African snake.
examples: The black *mamba* is one of the deadliest snakes alive.
*Mambas* can move faster than a person can run.
A green *mamba* was hiding in the branches.

gloss: A fast Cuban ballroom dance, or a piece of music written for it.
examples: They danced the *mambo* at the wedding.
She teaches a *mambo* class on Thursdays.
The band closed the night with two fast *mambos*.

gloss: An X-ray of the breast used to look for signs of cancer.
examples: She goes in for a *mammogram* every year.
The *mammogram* came back clear.
Insurance covers annual *mammograms* after forty.

gloss: A large extinct elephant with long curved tusks and a shaggy coat.
examples: A frozen *mammoth* was found in Siberia.
*Mammoths* died out only a few thousand years ago.
The museum has a full *mammoth* skeleton.

gloss: A circular design of symbols and patterns used in Hindu and Buddhist meditation and in art.
examples: The monks spent a week making a sand *mandala*.
She colors *mandalas* to relax.
The rug's pattern is based on a *mandala*.

gloss: A small sweet citrus fruit with loose skin that peels off easily.
examples: He packed two *mandarins* in her lunch.
The salad had *mandarin* segments in it.
*Mandarins* are in season around the holidays.
contrast: Capitalized, Mandarin is the main language of China — a completely different word from the fruit.

gloss: A small stringed instrument with a rounded back and paired strings, played with a pick.
examples: He plays *mandolin* in a bluegrass band.
Two *mandolins* carried the melody.
She bought a used *mandolin* at a pawn shop.

gloss: A hard gray metal used in making steel, and a mineral the body needs in small amounts.
examples: *Manganese* makes the steel much harder.
Whole grains are a good source of *manganese*.
The mine produces copper and *manganese*.

gloss: A tropical coastal tree that grows in salt water on tangled, arching roots.
examples: *Mangroves* protect the shoreline from storm surge.
We kayaked through a *mangrove* swamp.
Developers cleared the *mangroves* to build the resort.

gloss: The state of being an adult man, or the qualities traditionally associated with being a man.
examples: He reached *manhood* during the war.
The ceremony marks a boy's passage into *manhood*.
He felt that his *manhood* was being questioned.

gloss: An organized search by police for a person who is wanted or on the run.
examples: A statewide *manhunt* ended at a motel outside Reno.
The *manhunt* lasted six days.
Police launched two *manhunts* in the same week.

gloss: An extreme, obsessive enthusiasm for something, or a period of overexcited behavior in bipolar disorder.
examples: The country was gripped by tulip *mania*.
He has a *mania* for organizing things.
Her *mania* was followed by weeks of depression.

gloss: Someone who behaves in a wild, violent, or obsessive way.
examples: Some *maniac* was weaving through traffic.
He works like a *maniac* before every deadline.
The movie is about a *maniac* loose in a small town.

gloss: An official list of the cargo or passengers carried by a ship, plane, or truck.
examples: Customs checked the ship's *manifest*.
His name wasn't on the flight *manifest*.
The *manifests* showed twelve containers missing.

gloss: A pipe or chamber with several openings that collects or distributes gases in an engine.
examples: The exhaust *manifold* cracked.
Oil was leaking onto the intake *manifold*.
He replaced both *manifolds* on the old truck.

gloss: The act of controlling someone or something in a clever, often dishonest, way.
examples: The book is about media *manipulation*.
He was charged with market *manipulation*.
It felt less like advice and more like *manipulation*.

gloss: Someone who controls other people cleverly and dishonestly to get what they want.
examples: He's a skilled *manipulator*.
*Manipulators* rarely admit what they're doing.
She finally saw him for the *manipulator* he was.

gloss: Unexpected help or good fortune that arrives exactly when it is needed.
examples: The grant was *manna* to a program about to close.
Rain in August is *manna* for the corn crop.
For a struggling shop, the tourists were *manna* from heaven.

gloss: The way in which something is done, or the way a person behaves toward others.
examples: She has a calm, professional *manner*.
He answered in a rather cold *manner*.
It's bad *manners* to talk with your mouth full.
contrast: In the plural, manners usually means politeness, not just "ways of doing things".

gloss: A large country house with land around it, historically the home of a lord.
examples: The *manor* has been in the family for centuries.
They turned the old *manor* into a hotel.
Several *manors* in the county are open to visitors.
contrast: Sounds exactly like manner. A manor is a house; a manner is a way of doing something.

gloss: The thick layer of rock between the earth's crust and its core, or a role and responsibility passed from one person to another.
examples: Heat from the *mantle* drives the plates apart.
She took up the *mantle* of her mentor.
A *mantle* of snow covered the fields.
contrast: Don't confuse with mantel, the shelf above a fireplace — same pronunciation, different spelling and meaning.

gloss: A word or phrase repeated in meditation, or a saying someone repeats as a guiding principle.
examples: Her *mantra* is "measure twice, cut once."
He repeated the *mantra* under his breath.
"Location, location, location" is one of the oldest *mantras* in real estate.

gloss: A book of instructions explaining how to use or repair something.
examples: Check the owner's *manual* for the tire pressure.
The software came with a two-hundred-page *manual*.
He keeps all the appliance *manuals* in a drawer.

gloss: A hollow gourd or plastic shell filled with beads, shaken in pairs to make a rattling rhythm.
examples: She shook a pair of *maracas* in time with the band.
Every kid got a *maraca* in music class.
The *maracas* set the beat for the whole song.
